items.title: Compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates
items.detail: Cisco Talos is aware of eight intermediate certificates belonging to the intermediate certificate authority, eMudhra . Rather than possessing the mandatory 384 bits of pseudo-random security, several private keys evaluated single-digit and double-digit integers. This misconfiguration allows an attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs to impersonate any website or service. Six of the TLS certificates, trusted by Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple have been blocked by these vendors already. Two other certificates, used for codesigning by Microsoft, have also been blocked. Talos expects there will be additional patches available across a variety of technologies as software applications work to remediate the certificates’ exposure. Following the disclosure, eMudhra has revoked the compromised certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root. Compromise details The cause of this issue, originated during an April 30, 2025 key generation activity conducted by eMudhra under its emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and cross-signed Comodo AAA Certificate Services. During a key generation ceremony for 24 subordinate CAs, a flaw in eMudhra’s key generation process created a second set of weak P-384 keys during a wrap/unwrap step. Those keys were mistakenly used for eight intermediate CA certificates. This flaw took the encryption from 384 bytes of entropy down to 3 – 8, making recovering the private keys trivial. The following are the impacted certificates, as illustrated in Mozilla’s bug report : EM EV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV), CCADB A012304 SHA-256 E7568FE6E12331F4FD7DE61DA4C7559D0F8EB192A218D4741A3BA75184333838 serial c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3 EM OV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV), CCADB A012308 SHA-256 98B896625C0C230ADEEC3EB2CF6AAD5001ECF9156A68644E82374CE5833BC25B serial 6cada367fb1c100088120ea202d568, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3 EM DV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV), CCADB A012302 SHA-256 42C4ACCD12C4F59597925E1A08A7A90102608543809308D50EC427E118BA1493 serial a4aee678f23362b4c0e460b772f214, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3 EM EV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc), CCADB A012296 SHA-256 432EC25F0D28DE9006D97BF752F17BBB2CD41F669933FCB072D9A1148D0261F3 serial 8009928a64107601af05fa2f19f109, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3 EM OV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc), CCADB A012300 SHA-256 CB6E15165AC802E9B3F993F16C25D41F4E81C21EBDE71AE1B012AC00BF9C7C3F serial 296926c227a3a1526392b19482a504, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3 EM DV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc), CCADB A012294 SHA-256 0164D7CEAE5BB909C272AF151FF44B1177AE9B47D9424B94F1D9558C30934D19 serial 588b2e3c2bb8cda13e1a1209254321, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3 EM OV CS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV), CCADB A012306 SHA-256 9E39DE2881273ACC225A149C72BA3E0F51424963669AB633EE1DC7DF5DB067B4 serial 7818933f8f85b4619a2b35fba83d0a, issuer emSign Root CS CA - G3 EM OV CS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc), CCADB A012298 SHA-256 4B2460A466F95FD40113BCDCCA2CEB29B3B093921DE45474DA7DF48874C630B1 serial 544b7f922c31ae220a4a922916f6e6, issuer emSign Root CS CA - G3 CVE-2026-111943 Unlike languages that defer entirely to external dynamic system libraries (like OpenSSL), the Go programming runtime implements its own X.509 chain verification engine in the standard library (crypto/x509). While Go usually queries platform certificates, several platforms or static container environments rely on embedded or legacy root certificate pools where certificate revocations are ignored. To eliminate exploitation across the entire cloud-native ecosystem including Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, and Prometheus, the Go team designated the compromised certificates as a vulnerability, CVE-2026-111943, and released Go versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10. The fixed versions filter out chains containingthe SHA-256 hashes of the SubjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI) for all eight compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates. Impact These compromised certificates could allow adversaries to impersonate servers and intercept or modify traffic. The impact of their exposure is far more than just web browsers. Other programs that check for TLS certificates might still be impacted since they may not check revocation lists. One clear example is related to virtual private networks (VPNs); these technologies will likely require software updates to mitigate the issue. Based on this guidance, Talos strongly recommends users update software using and handling TLS certificates as fixes become available. Talos is actively monitoring the impact of these compromised certificates and has not seen any malicious incidents involving them in the wild yet (as of October 21, 2026 14:00 UTC / 10:00 a.m. ET). Significance of this breach Public key infrastructure relies on trust being delegated through certificate chains: root CAs authorize intermediate CAs, which can issue certificates within the scope of their authority. An attacker who obtains an intermediate CA’s private key may be able to issue fraudulent certificates that clients accept, subject to the intermediate certificate’s constraints and each client’s validation controls. In this incident, six compromised intermediates were for TLS and two were for code signing. For TLS, an attacker able to intercept or redirect a connection could use a fraudulent certificate to impersonate a server and potentially read or modify traffic if the client still trusts the affected key and no applicable protection blocks it. Protections such as revocation, key distrust, certificate transparency enforcement, and certificate pinning can prevent or expose such an attack. Browser vendors have blocked the affected TLS keys, but other applications may rely on separate trust stores or validation paths: Enterprise infrastructure and VPNs Organizations should assess TLS-using software and appliances, including proxies, reverse load balancers, VPN clients, and gateways. Exposure depends on the certificate chain being validated and the trust store and revocation behavior in use. A stale or separately managed trust store may need an application, operating-system, firmware, or trust-bundle update; verify the required action for each product. Software supply chains and CI/CD Build runners and package managers may be exposed if they fetch content over TLS while still trusting an affected key and an attacker can intercept the connection. A fraudulent TLS certificate could enable registry impersonation, but it would not by itself bypass separate package integrity checks, such as lockfile hashes, checksums, signatures, or provenance controls. Assess the actual package-manager configuration and dependency path. Industrial IoT and embedded systems Review devices that use bundled or independently managed CA stores, especially where certificate revocation or trust-store updates may be limited. Some devices may require a vendor update or compensating control, but the necessary action depends on each device’s validation and update mechanisms. Talos recommends updating affected software and trust stores as vendor fixes become available. Coverage The following SNORT® SIDs provide coverage for this threat: 67363 - 67374. Talos would like to highlight the efforts of Chris Morrison for providing emergency coverage and mitigations for this threat.

items.title: Two critical RCEs in PHP core
items.detail: Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of two unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) flaws in PHP core, dubbed “php2shell”, triggered by a plain HTTP request and exploitable before any application code runs, affecting every PHP build since 5.4. Based on the entities involved in the disclosure, artificial intelligence and associated technologies played a key role in the discovery of these vulnerabilities — yet another example of how these technologies are forcing change across the landscape, most notably on patching processes for organizations because of the wave of vulnerabilities being disclosed. Cisco customers are covered with the Cisco Talos Network Intrusion Prevention (SNORT®) signatures 67359 and 67360. These rules are also available in the Community Ruleset for open-source customers. Please refer to the following recommendations, detection, and coverage guidance for more information. Details CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are both critical vulnerabilities with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. CVE-2026-109618 occurs when out-of-memory handling interrupts PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat invalid data as valid. CVE-2026-109619 occurs when a stale internal state is reused after its backing memory has already been freed, before normal initialization resets it. Impact The potential blast radius is enormous and extends across the PHP ecosystem. The vulnerability sits in PHP core, so applications running affected versions — including WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Shopware, WooCommerce, and Laravel, plus PHP sites hosted through cPanel or Plesk — may be exposed. Note that many older branches will no longer receive fixes, so customers are urged to upgrade to a supported version as soon as possible. Talos regularly investigates threat actor exploitation of vulnerabilities. State-sponsored and affiliated threat actors, as well as ransomware and other financially motivated groups, all employ tactics to exploit RCE. Talos assesses that all industries running PHP applications are at risk for exploitation if systems remain unpatched. PHP 8.1 and older are end of life (EOL), and PHP 8.2 security support ends Dec. 31, 2026. Talos’ initial estimates based on open-source intelligence show a significant corpus of PHP systems that will not receive a patch (~50%). If your organization is running PHP 8.1 or older, Talos very strongly advises immediate update to PHP 8.2 or later. There is no patch for PHP 8.1 or older. Talos is actively monitoring the impact of these CVEs and has not seen them being exploited in the wild yet (as of October 21, 2026 14:00 UTC/10:00 a.m. ET). Recommendations and detection guidance Talos strongly recommends all PHP users to upgrade to the available fixed releases . There are no intermediate or temporary controls that provide comprehensive protection; however, PHP advises that the following measure may reduce exposure to specific attack paths: CVE-2026-109618 Set memory_limit=-1, preferably in a way applications can't override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path. Set a low post_max_size. For applications that don't require file uploads, set post_max_size = 8M. If file uploads are necessary, set post_max_size = 32M. Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Consider enforcing limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth. These limits must also cover requests without a usable Content-Length. Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, as these can cause the vulnerable allocation failure. CVE-2026-109619 Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. Use php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on ini_set() or FPM .user.ini. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants. On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only. Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors, or @ does not help. Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts, including failures in callbacks, upload or import processing, and cleanup. This is another vulnerability that owes its origin to AI and its associated technologies. As we move through 2026, the wave of vulnerabilities and related patches is building. Talos advises organizations to work on a triaged process for prioritizing vulnerabilities with a specific focus on public-facing systems and vulnerabilities that are under active exploitation. The glaring need to prioritize vulnerabilities along with a streamlined process for rolling out patching strongly indicates that the historic trend of “baking in” patches before deployment is not going to survive the AI era. The true impact of this vulnerability will take time to evaluate. These types of vulnerabilities that impact core technologies tend to cascade into other platforms and applications as they evaluate impact and provide associated patching, harkening back to the waves of exploitation that we saw after Log4J. Coverage SNORT® SIDs covering these vulnerabilities for subscribers: 67359, 67360, 67375. Free community rules are live through our Community Ruleset . Talos would like to highlight the efforts of Ankur Tyagi, Dalton Schaadt, Brandon Stultz, and Matt Killion for providing emergency coverage and mitigations for these threats.

items.title: Parasitizing trust: How legitimate infrastructure becomes a delivery pipeline for attackers
items.detail: Legitimate infrastructure has become a powerful delivery mechanism for attackers, carrying the inherent trust they once had to build. As Cisco Talos explored in our previous research on weaponizing software-as-a-service (SaaS) notification pipelines , these platforms are increasingly repurposed as proxies for malicious intent. Talos has since tracked a significant acceleration in this trend, observing abuse across more than 25 distinct legitimate platforms in the past year. The abused infrastructure included collaboration, productivity, file-sharing, survey, payment and AI-related platforms. This demonstrates that attackers are not limiting themselves to traditional phishing infrastructure or lookalike domains. Instead, they are systematically subverting the very tools businesses trust. Order notification abuse Talos recently analyzed two order notification campaigns abusing Staples and Dell transactional email pipelines. Together, these campaigns accounted for roughly 1,400 messages observed by Talos. The malicious element was not the outer sender identity, like a simple forged sender or lookalike domain. It was the content of the legitimate order notification workflow rendered. The suspicious content appeared inside the notification itself, in fields that would normally contain shipping information. The attacker’s objective was to use a trusted retail pipeline to create urgency around a high-value purchase and push the recipient toward an attacker-controlled phone number. In the first campaign, the message appeared as a Staples order confirmation from "support@orders.staples.com” with the subject line, “Here’s your Staples order #9939818875. Thanks for shopping with us.” The body displayed a plausible purchase for an Apple iPad, including order number, delivery timing, pricing, billing information and standard Staples footer content. The suspicious element was embedded in the order details: “Helpline 806 283 7712,” “Order Confirmed,” and the Staples corporate address appeared in fields normally associated with shipping or billing information. Figure 1. Staples order notification The structure of the message matters. The attacker was not trying to persuade the user to click a crude phishing link. Instead, the message created the impression that an expensive order had already been placed and that the fastest way to resolve it was to call the embedded “helpline.” The desired user action was a phone call. Once the victim moved from email to voice, the attacker could continue the scam through social engineering, payment manipulation, credential theft, or remote assistance fraud. The headers reinforced the trust problem. The Staples message showed DKIM alignment for “orders.staples.com” and DMARC passed for the visible Staples domain. The message also passed through forwarding and re-encapsulation paths, including Proton Mail, Microsoft 365, and downstream enterprise mail infrastructure. These hops complicate provenance analysis, but they do not change the core issue: Authentication helped establish that the outer message was credible, while offering no assurance that the phone number or transaction context was legitimate. The second campaign used the same pattern in a Dell order received notification. The message was sent from “Dell | Order Received <received@order.dellcom>” with the subject line, “We have your order | Dell Purchase ID: 2009829958247.” The body presented a purchase for Microsoft Project Standard 2024, totaling $736.09. As with the Staples example, the suspicious content appeared in transaction fields. The “Ship To” and “Bill To” sections included “Confirmed Order,” “Helpline 808 232 6397,” and “Call Our Sales Team”. The Dell message used the same psychological lever: an unexpected high-value purchase, a legitimate-looking order template, and a phone number positioned as the path to resolution. The attacker did not need the recipient to trust a new domain or unfamiliar brand. The message borrowed credibility from Dell’s order pipeline and redirected the recipient toward attacker-controlled contact information. Authentication results showed DKIM passing for Dell-related infrastructure and DMARC passing for “order.dell.com”. As with the Staples sample, forwarding artifacts and SRS-style return paths appeared as the message moved through Microsoft and enterprise mail infrastructure. But the malicious intent did not live in an obviously forged sender. It lived inside the rendered order content. Figure 2. Dell order notification These campaigns illustrate the same trust-boundary failure described in our earlier research on platform-as-a-proxy (PaaP) abuse. In those cases, attackers placed malicious content into SaaS fields that trusted platforms later rendered into notifications. Here, the same concept appears in commerce infrastructure, in the retailer’s order pipeline. The attacker supplies the intent, while the trusted system performs the delivery. From a defensive perspective, sender authentication is necessary, but it is not sufficient. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC help answer whether a message came from expected infrastructure. However, they do not answer whether the transaction was legitimate, whether the rendered fields make business sense, or whether the user is being pushed toward an attacker-controlled action. Order notifications should be treated as sensitive content. Any field reflected into a transactional message — shipping name, billing name, address line, company name, order note, support field, or fulfillment instruction — can become a delivery vehicle if it is not validated before rendering. Retailers and security teams should correlate order notification content with account history, payment state, shipping context, and known support channels. Transactional templates should reject or flag unexpected phone numbers, URLs, urgency language, and support instructions when they appear in fields where they do not belong. In both campaigns, the wrapper was legitimate enough to inherit trust. The payload was attacker-influenced. That distinction is the center of this attack class. The abuse of commerce pipelines is merely one manifestation of a broader, systemic vulnerability. Whether the attacker initiates a fake purchase or a fraudulent account sign-up, the root cause remains the same: Platforms are implicitly trusting data that enters their systems from untrusted sources, only to render that data into high-reputation, automated notifications. This same mechanism of reflection — where input is echoed back into an email to a third party — is the engine behind an evolution in list bombing, moving the attack from simple denial-of-service to a sophisticated vehicle for content delivery. List bombing: From inbox disruption to content delivery List bombing is an abuse technique in which attackers submit a victim’s email address to numerous legitimate registration, subscription or notification workflows, flooding the inbox with automated messages. While this vector is traditionally viewed as a denial-of-service or distraction tactic designed to bury critical alerts in a flood of junk, Talos has observed a subset of cases where this behavior is being repurposed as a delivery vehicle for malicious content. This abuse occurs when an attacker identifies public-facing registration, profile, or project-naming forms that lack sufficient input validation. By inputting a "hostile string" — such as a cryptocurrency-themed lure — into fields intended for a name, company, or title, the attacker forces the platform to treat this data as legitimate user information. When the service reflexively incorporates this input into its automated welcome, verification, or notification templates, the system acts as an unintended carrier, delivering the attacker’s content inside a high-reputation, system-generated email that can pass standard authentication checks. The attacker’s objective in these cases is to bypass the security perimeter by laundering their malicious content through the brand reputation of a trusted service provider. While this is not yet a broad industry shift, it represents a calculated abuse of a platform's trust boundary. By embedding their lure in an automated notification, the adversary ensures that the message arrives with the appearance of administrative legitimacy, significantly increasing the likelihood that the recipient will trust the content. The goal is to reach the target's inbox with enough platform authority that the message may be evaluated as routine notification traffic rather than attacker-controlled content. Figure 3. Registration field reflection Beyond the risk to the individual recipient, this vector creates a significant brand liability. When a service provider’s infrastructure is used to broadcast fraudulent content, the resulting user complaints and bounce-backs can degrade the platform's own sender reputation, potentially triggering blocklisting that impacts their legitimate business communications. Bounce abuse: When delivery reports carry the lure The final vector moves the abuse pattern into the mail system itself. Instead of relying on a retailer, SaaS platform, or registration workflow to generate the message, the attacker attempts to make a delivery status workflow carry attacker-controlled content. Bounces, formally known as delivery status notifications (DSNs) or non-delivery reports (NDRs), are generated when a message cannot be delivered. Under normal conditions, a mail system sends the delivery report back to the original SMTP envelope sender. Depending on the implementation, that report may include the original headers, portions of the message body, URLs, attachments, or an encapsulated copy of the failed message. That returned content creates the abuse opportunity. In one example Talos observed, a mail delivery system notification carried a WeTransfer-themed file-sharing lure. The administrative wrapper made the message look like routine mail-system noise, while the nested content asked the recipient to engage with what appeared to be a file transfer workflow. The attacker’s goal was to make the phishing lure feel less like an unsolicited external message and more like part of a technical delivery failure that required review. Users are conditioned to view system errors as benign and are far more likely to engage with an "administrative" fix than a suspicious, standalone phishing email. Figure 4. Bounce carrying a file-sharing lure There are several ways this kind of message can reach a victim. In opportunistic backscatter, an attacker sends mail using the victim’s address as the forged envelope sender. If an intermediate system accepts the message and later fails to deliver it, the resulting DSN may be sent back to the forged sender. If the DSN includes enough of the original message, the bounce itself can carry the lure. A second possibility is intentional bounce abuse, where the attacker uses an authenticated, compromised, or otherwise controllable sending context to trigger a delivery failure that returns attacker-influenced content. This differs from an outright forged NDR, where the attacker simply fabricates the bounce message and sends it directly. From the recipient’s mailbox, however, these cases can look similar: A delivery-failure wrapper contains content the attacker wants the user to trust. This distinction matters for defenders. A DSN’s administrative appearance does not validate the content inside it. The outer message may be a legitimate delivery report, while the returned or encapsulated content may still contain a phishing link, credential harvesting page, malicious attachment, or social engineering prompt. The content-trust gap: A defensive imperative Across these vectors, the defensive failure is consistent: Trusted infrastructure is being treated as a shortcut for trusted content. Sender authentication remains essential. SPF, DKIM, DMARC, reputation, and infrastructure analysis help determine whether a message came from an expected source. But these controls do not answer a separate and increasingly important question: What was that trusted system instructed to carry? Order notifications, registration workflows and delivery reports all create opportunities for attacker-influenced content to appear inside messages that users and security tools are conditioned to trust. In the Staples and Dell campaigns, the suspicious content was a phone number placed into transactional fields. In list bombing and registration abuse, the lure can appear inside reflected account or profile data. In bounce abuse, the malicious content may sit inside returned message data or a nested MIME object. Defending against this requires content-aware validation at multiple points in the delivery chain. Platform owners should treat any user-controlled value rendered into an email template as untrusted data. Fields used for names, addresses, company names, project titles, order notes or support instructions should be validated before storage and again before rendering. Phone numbers, URLs, markup, line breaks, and urgent support language should be rejected or flagged when they appear in fields where they do not belong. Security gateways should inspect the fully rendered message, not only the sender or template. That includes HTML, text, URLs, redirects, attachments, personalization fields, and nested MIME content. For transactional email, defenders should also evaluate whether the message content aligns with the workflow that produced it. An order notification containing unexpected support numbers, cancellation instructions, or high-urgency language should be treated differently from a routine receipt. For delivery reports, recursive MIME inspection is especially important. Gateways should parse DSN containers, extract returned messages or message fragments, and apply normal phishing, malware, and URL analysis to the nested content. A bounce should explain a delivery failure, not provide a blind path for untrusted payloads. The broader lesson is that attackers are no longer only exploiting technical vulnerabilities in infrastructure. They are exploiting the assumptions built into business processes. When legitimate systems render attacker-influenced data into trusted notifications, the result can pass authentication checks and still deliver malicious intent. Defenders should therefore treat sender trust and content trust as separate but complementary signals. The wrapper can explain where a message came from. It cannot prove that the payload is safe. items.title: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise
items.detail: In this article What’s happening What is ARTEX? Mitigation and protection guidance References Learn more As early as September 2026, Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, used the agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries. Several of these Storm-0940 ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the actor obtaining privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure – including multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours. Microsoft assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible for the recently disclosed ConnectWise supply chain compromise of a multi-tenant application. This activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and allows them to scale their operations exponentially. Agents are not constrained by factors affecting humans – they can work around the clock, on weekends, and on holidays and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously enabling significantly reduced time from selecting a target to achieving objectives, increasing the speed and impact of complex attacks like supply chain compromises. Storm-0940’s use of ARTEX accelerated the speed of compromised application abuse to authenticate to Microsoft 365 customer environments through applications that had already been granted access. This allowed the threat actor to operate without requiring an interactive user sign-in. In multiple affected environments, Microsoft observed AI-accelerated follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access. The activity conducted by the threat actor through the usage of ARTEX framework did not result from a compromise of or a vulnerability in Microsoft corporate systems, products, or services. Although Microsoft identified Storm-0940-initiated authentication and follow-on activity in multiple customer environments, the presence of an affected application or successful threat actor authentication does not necessarily indicate that customer data was accessed or exfiltrated. Microsoft Defender XDR provides detections and hunting queries for suspicious Microsoft Graph activity and activity associated with known threat infrastructure. Customers should review service principal sign-ins, investigate unexpected application credential or privilege changes, and follow ConnectWise’s published containment guidance while preserving relevant evidence for investigation. For a full list of detections please see the detections section. What’s happening Storm-0940 is a China-state aligned actor (with no known industry aliases) that has been active since 2021 and targets organizations across multiple industries for data theft. The actor has historically gained initial access using password spraying and exploitation of internet-facing applications, before using compromised accounts to move through targeted environments. In cloud environments, the actor has also established persistence by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications, allowing continued access to Microsoft 365 resources. The actor has used these applications to access and exfiltrate email and other data through Microsoft Graph. As early as September 2026, Storm-0940 used the agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries. These include aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits. During the ConnectWise supply chain compromise, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate scanning and reconnaissance, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse at downstream victims. Several of these Storm-0940 ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the actor obtaining privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure – including multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours. When automated with AI, these activities generate a large volume of traffic and log data that may generate alerts. However, the speed of the activity allows very little time for Defenders to respond to those alerts and remediate the actor’s access in a coordinated fashion. Storm-0940’s activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations. While the majority of the targeting wasn’t successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time. What is ARTEX? ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing framework that can use any AI model to automate a variety of offensive security workflows. The ARTEX framework is a multi-agent LLM system written in GO with a Next.js frontend. While the UI and generated output default to English, the framework can be switched to Korean, Mandarin, Spanish, or Japanese. ARTEX is a system of LLM-driven agents that run an autonomous penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction. The agents then accumulate the discovered assets and vulnerabilities into a graph during the penetration test. In October 2026, public reporting noted that the ARTEX framework was being used by threat actors, such as the personal data breaches targeting Korean financial institutions. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified threat actors across multiple geographic regions leveraging the ARTEX framework. On October 16, 2026, ConnectWise publicly reported unauthorized access to its customers’ tenants using multiple OAuth application identities. Following the unauthorized access, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to reach more than 2,250 tenants at 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute, a pace that leaves defenders with little time to detect and respond. While OAuth application abuse is a typical part of Storm-0940’s toolset, in this case the actor used ARTEX to accelerate the activity to machine speed. Figure 1. Scale and speed of a subset of Storm-0940’s automated ARTEX campaign on downstream tenants, including tenant reach and rapid sign-ins. Password Spraying Between October 10 and 14, 2026, Storm-0940 infrastructure at 144.172.64[.]99 conducted an automated cross-tenant password-spray campaign targeting 327 accounts across eight organizations to gain access to Microsoft 365 and Exchange Online. During this large campaign, Microsoft telemetry captured 151,000+ failed logon events, with activity peaking on October 11 at 2,900 failures per minute and concentrating more than 111,000 failures into a single day. The campaign blended broad, low-rate account spraying with sustained, high-volume authentication attempts against selected identities; 48 accounts received more than 1,000 failures, and lockout responses represented nearly 98% of all activity. Despite the scale, no successful authentication, token issuance, Graph call, or directory change was observed. Downstream customer access On October 15, immediately after this notable activity, public reports of the compromise of the popular cloud backup application ConnectWise started to surface with direct references to indicators of compromise matching the same network range observed for the earlier password-spray campaign (144.172.64.x). An advisory from the affected cloud backup vendor posted on October 16 shared later additional indicators with one IP address matching exactly the 144.172.64[.]99 infrastructure responsible for the earlier password-spray campaign. Additionally, after acquiring control of the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications, the AI agents operating on behalf of the threat actor continued to use the same IP range to authenticate to customer environments using the illicit access acquired through these stolen app credentials, effectively taking advantage of the already established trust by these apps within a tenant. In some of these environments, the AI agents (on behalf of the threat actor) progressed beyond authentication to Microsoft Graph and directory operations, including reconnaissance, application credential modifications to establish persistence, and changes involving identities, groups, and privileged roles. Microsoft identified multiple customer environments with evidence of follow-on activity, highlighting how a compromised third-party application with high privileges could provide access beyond its originally intended purpose. The application credential modification made by Storm-0940’s associated agents in the targeted victims’ environments can lead to persistence through other identities, credentials, and cloud services. These changes can remain active as a backdoor even after the original compromised application is mediated. Organizations should examine service principal sign-ins alongside subsequent Microsoft Graph activity, directory changes, and resource access, correlating suspicious events with authorized administrative activity. The presence of an affected application, or even successful authentication, does not necessarily indicate unauthorized data access or data exfiltration. Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations. Immediate actions Keep affected ConnectWise application connections disabled until ConnectWise provides formal restoration instructions. Do not delete enterprise applications as the first response. Preserve configuration and evidence before making irreversible changes. Inventory all four application IDs listed in this profile and record the local service-principal Object ID in each tenant. Review every Microsoft 365 tenant where the affected applications are currently or were previously installed or authorized, even if the integration is no longer in use. Search by application ID rather than display name. Preserve available Microsoft Entra sign-in and audit records , Microsoft Purview Audit records, SIEM data, and previously configured Microsoft Graph telemetry. Do not delay urgent containment while waiting for exports. Review activity starting from at least October 15, 2026. Where records are available, extend service-principal sign-in review to October 1 and investigate earlier related activity, including failed authentications and volume anomalies. Review successful and failed service-principal sign-ins separately. Investigate unfamiliar sources and activity outside expected vendor infrastructure; do not limit review to the published IPs. Review Microsoft Entra audit records for application or service-principal credential additions; new applications, service principals, or owners; app-role assignments and consent grants; privileged role assignments; and changes to users, groups, authentication methods, or Conditional Access. On confirmed suspicious activity, revoke unnecessary permissions and rotate credentials. Review Microsoft 365 audit records to look for reconnaissance activities like listing directories, permissions, and approvals coming from unusual IPs. Review Microsoft 365 audit records for unusual mail or file access, downloads, forwarding, inbox or transport rules, delegated mailbox permissions, and related resource activity. Preserve evidence, then have an appropriately authorized responder remove confirmed unauthorized credentials, grants, owners, assignments, and identities. Additional recommendations Threat actor misuse of AI accelerates risk across enterprise environments by amplifying existing threats such as exploitation of vulnerabilities, phishing, malware threats, and insider activity. To help organizations stay ahead of AI-enabled threat activity, Microsoft has introduced the Security Dashboard for AI . The dashboard provides users with a unified view of AI security posture by aggregating security, identity, and data risk across Microsoft Defender , Microsoft Entra , and Microsoft Purview . This allows organizations to understand what AI assets exist in their environment, recognize emerging risk patterns, and prioritize governance and security across AI agents, applications, and platforms. To learn more about the Microsoft Security Dashboard for AI see: Assess your organization’s AI risk with Microsoft Security Dashboard for AI (Preview) . Enable threat protection for AI services in Microsoft Defender for Cloud to identify threats to generative AI applications in real time and for assistance in responding to security issues. Apply least privilege to multi-tenant application permissions and consent grants. Monitor credential additions, privilege assignments, and anomalous app-only activity, especially to applications with high privileged permissions and scopes. Verify that vendor credential rotation and any tenant-level remediation eliminated remaining unauthorized access. Assess the operational effect on backup and restore workflows and follow current ConnectWise restoration guidance. Microsoft Defender XDR detections Microsoft Defender XDR customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender XDR coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog. Customers with provisioned access can also use Microsoft Security Copilot in Microsoft Defender to investigate and respond to incidents, hunt for threats, and protect their organization with relevant threat intelligence. items.title: Critical RCE vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
items.detail: Vulnerability overview On October 20, 2026, the PHP security team published a preliminary notice regarding an upcoming emergency release that addresses two critical vulnerabilities (both rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale). The patches were released on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at 14:00 UTC. The release was expedited after information about the vulnerabilities was leaked to the public before the scheduled embargo was lifted. In a post on Hacker News, a user reported two RCE vulnerabilities in PHP, allegedly affecting all versions starting with PHP 5.4.0. The vulnerabilities in question are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Shortly after the post appeared, researchers confirmed the existence of the vulnerabilities. Along with the leak of details, an exploit unofficially named PHP2Shell appeared online. In the leaked demo video, the exploit is shown in action on web servers running WordPress, MediaWiki, phpBB, Magento, Joomla, Laravel, Symfony, Drupal, and WHMCS — platforms that power many modern websites. The authenticity of the demonstration and the exact behavior of the exploit had not been independently verified at the time of publication. According to the researcher who published the PoC, the vulnerabilities are related to the handling of the multipart/form-data MIME type in conjunction with the session upload progress mechanism ( session.upload_progress ) in the PHP core and fall under the categories of use-after-free and memory corruption. This means that the flaws cannot be patched via application code, and the only possible fix is to update PHP on the server. The attack works without authentication: an attacker with network access to a PHP application can execute arbitrary code on behalf of the PHP process without needing to authenticate. Security advisories issued by PHP on October 21 confirm this information. The vulnerabilities affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8. As of this publication, branches from 8.2 to 8.5 are supported. Older branches, including PHP 8.1, 8.0, 7.x, and 5.x, have reached the end of their lifecycle; however, due to the critical severity of the vulnerabilities, backported patches have also been released for versions 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Sansec experts estimate that widespread exploitation could begin within 15 minutes of the update’s release. We strongly recommend that administrators responsible for publicly accessible PHP web servers take the following steps before the patch is available: Conduct an inventory of all PHP-based systems in the infrastructure (including web servers, control panels, third-party software, etc.). Disable upload-progress: set session.upload_progress.enabled = Off using the php_admin_flag in PHP-FPM pools. Block multipart requests on nginx and Apache servers. Consider temporarily isolating PHP applications that connect to the Internet until fixes are released. Ensure readiness to install the patch immediately upon its release. Plan to migrate servers running unsupported versions (8.1 and earlier) to the latest PHP branch. Detection by Kaspersky solutions Kaspersky solutions detect the described malicious activity at various stages of the attack. Possible detection scenarios are listed below. When an attempt is made to exploit these RCE vulnerabilities, Kaspersky Endpoint Detection and Response promptly alerts the user to suspicious actions performed in the context of a web server, on both Linux and Windows machines. This activity is detected by the following rules: creating_windows_shell_from_a_web_servers_process ; possible_web_shell_creating_via_exploit ; spawning_process_from_webserver_more_filters_linux ; webserver_interpreter_execution_linux ; executable_file_in_www_folder . Detection of the PHP2Shell vulnerability exploit by KEDR Exploitation of the PHP2Shell vulnerability in network traffic is detected by Kaspersky Anti Targeted Attack (KATA) . This solution detects such activity with the following verdicts: Exploit.CVE-2026-109618.HTTP.C&C and Exploit.CVE-2026-109619.HTTP.C&C . Detection of the PHP2Shell vulnerability exploit by KATA Our Kaspersky Endpoint Security solution, now available as Kaspersky Next , also detects malicious post-exploitation activity using the Behavior Detection component , such as PDM:Exploit.Linux.Generic and PDM:Exploit.Win32.Generic.

items.title: Operation FlashHole: Lazarus breaks security, defies control
items.detail: In January, we responded to the Lazarus Group’s novel attack campaign against South Korea, which followed last year’s Operation SyncHole . In this new operation, the group employed an updated malware chain that included both their old and new malware, which we disclosed in full, and used another mandatory South Korean security software program as a part of infection chain using a watering‑hole strategy. Notably, the group targeted victims more selectively, sending spear‑phishing emails with links to fabricated but relevant sites, such as portfolio and résumé pages tailored to each target. We dubbed this activity Operation FlashHole. Operation FlashHole attack flow during initial compromise Our examination reveals that the earliest evidence of this new operation dates back to July 2025. This suggests the group began preparing for the campaign shortly after ending Operation SyncHole, which lasted at least four months. We identified a minimum of three organizations impacted by the campaign in South Korea’s software, construction, and wired communication equipment manufacturing sectors. These sectors differ from those affected by Operation SyncHole, indicating that the group has expanded its target scope over time. Background After more than a year since the first observation of Operation SyncHole, we detected a suspicious execution chain originating from legitimate South Korean software. This chain mirrors the one from the previous operation; however, this time, the attacker abused CrossWeb EX instead of Cross EX, which was abused in Operation SyncHole. Both applications appear to be maintained by the same vendor, and both are related to financial security. CrossWeb EX is a financial security solution that is required to access widely used online banking and government websites. It encrypts communications between the user’s browser and the web server using public key infrastructure (PKI). This is not the first time Lazarus has abused this software. It was also used in 2021 to deploy the Racket downloader and again in 2022 and 2023 . Although the exact method by which CrossWeb EX was abused remains unclear, we determined that the attack chain ultimately leads to the execution of the malware in memory. We noted that the spawned process was running with a high integrity level. The parent process, INISAFECrossWebEXSvc.exe , originates from the installation bundle of INISAFE CrossWeb EX V3 version 3.4.1.2, released in 2023 after KrCERT’s public advisory . As we already mentioned in our SyncHole blog post, this pattern closely mirrors the long‑standing strategy employed by the Lazarus Group to target South Korea. Since CrossWeb EX and similar software is mandatory for South Korean users and typically runs in the background to interact with the browser, it has been leveraged as a critical attack vector by the group. In 2025, a paper was presented at the USENIX Security Symposium that investigated vulnerabilities in South Korea’s mandatory security software and demonstrated how such software can unintentionally create a massive attack surface. In July 2026, the South Korean government and several local security vendors also published a joint security advisory covering typical Lazarus attack techniques, including exploitation of financial security software. While this advisory overlaps with our findings from Operation FlashHole and Operation SyncHole, and AhnLab’s detailed analysis report Operation Double Barrel covers a wide range of recent Lazarus Group activities, we are conducting a more granular classification based on their TTPs. Initial infection vector Although we could not precisely determine what triggered the infection chain, our analysis uncovered a suspicious website hosted on GitHub Pages that is associated with the GitHub account used as the C2 channel. The GitHub account was created last September, and the initial version of the site was designed to showcase the résumé of a senior network appliance developer. In January, however, this site was replaced with another featuring an interior design showcase. The first site was likely accessed by an employee of a wired communication manufacturing company, while the second site likely affected a target in the construction sector. Appearance of the malicious websites The first site with the résumé had a photograph supposedly of a job seeker, but the lack of EXIF metadata and the unnatural texture of the image indicate that it was generated by AI. This suggests the Lazarus Group has incorporated AI into its long‑standing strategy, like other Korean‑speaking threat actors ( 1 , 2 ). The group most likely also used AI to create the lure site: the job seeker’s name resembles the Korean version of “John Doe,” and the portfolio was populated with seemingly meaningless details and random companies. The generated site was then manually tailored to specific targets. Suspected use of an AI-generated image on the résumé site The websites contained embedded links that loaded an external JavaScript file via a script tag. The research results showed a high possibility that visiting the malicious site initiated an infection process involving CrossWeb EX software. This assessment aligns with Lazarus’s recent approach, as detailed in the joint advisory published by the South Korean government and security companies. Full infection chain Following the initial compromise, the legitimate Windows binary fsquirt.exe was executed under the CrossWeb EX process and injected with shellcode containing a malicious DLL – TechHub malware. From our extensive and thorough examination, we identified several malicious payloads and reconstructed the complete infection chain. The infection chain is rather complex and reveals the Lazarus Group’s advanced operational techniques on targeted hosts. These techniques conceal their malicious payloads, intent and their sophisticated malware delivery framework. The latter was updated extensively compared to the previous campaign, despite the new operation starting less than a year later. Significantly, the execution chain below exists only in memory during the initial infiltration, highlighting the attackers’ considerable efforts to hide the initial compromise. Initial infection chain Following the initial compromise, the group sought to maintain persistence on the network by installing a pair of malware strains – TouchHub and TouchShift – leveraging DLL side‑loading under the name mscoree.dll . TouchHub was deployed by the first instance of TechHub. It then used DLL side-loading to launch TouchShift, which led to the in‑memory execution of another TechHub instance. After launching the second time, TechHub deployed another pair, ClientHub and LPEClient, rather than executing Cubridge directly. Only minimal traces of these files were found on disk; the remainder of the malicious code persisted exclusively in memory. Expanded infection chain after gaining persistence Since Cubridge remains only in memory at the initial compromise stage, we suspect the group designed this indirect, multistage chain to deliberately redeploy Cubridge after gaining persistence, as it serves as the most sophisticated orchestrator of the attack. Malware set The full chain comprises advanced variants of the known Lazarus malware strains, including TechHub, Cubridge, TouchShift, LPEClient, and the newly identified TouchHub and ClientHub. TechHub – the start of the chain TechHub, a downloader that plays a central role in this attack, communicates with GitHub using a Personal Access Token (PAT). It serves as the initial payload, providing the top of the chain with sufficient functionality to profile compromised hosts and facilitate subsequent payloads. This variant is a more advanced version of the malware named CLOUDBURST by Mandiant and NickelLoader by ESET. According to their reports, the earlier version communicated with a C2 server via HTTP(S) to fetch additional payloads. The latest iteration we found, however, communicates with GitHub instead and has updated command strings. We identified three variants of TechHub in the chain: an in‑memory version, a simple DLL side‑loading version, and a DLL side‑loading version that uses a registered Windows service. Depending on which stage loads the malware, it contacts a private GitHub repository via the GitHub API using either hard‑coded credentials or credentials retrieved from its configuration file. When TechHub loads, it creates a 4‑byte hexadecimal identifier (ID) in the range 0x1000–0xFFFF or reads one from the configuration file, enabling the attackers to distinguish between compromised hosts. TechHub then checks a GitHub issue by sending the request GET /issues?state=[open/closed] to determine whether any previous communication remains active and removes any traces of it if found. It then proceeds with the handshaking process. It creates a new issue titled 1[ID] with the body “hel” using the POST /issues request, and sets its status to open. It then retrieves a file from the repository containing the 2[ID] value in its name. This file contains the RSA public key. It generates a random 16‑byte XOR key, encrypts it with the provided RSA public key, and uploads the result, prefixed with 1[ID] , to the repository. The hard‑coded IV is XORed with the generated 16‑byte key and then used after the handshake. During file exchange, filenames follow the pattern [1|2][ID][random-16-byte-key] throughout communication. The “2” prefix indicates delivery from the repository to TechHub, while “1” indicates delivery from TechHub to the repository. The random 16‑byte key in the filename is used for AES encryption or decryption of each file’s contents, employing either a hard‑coded IV or an updated IV. After the key exchange is complete, TechHub reads a file with the prefix “2” once again and verifies that the delivered data equals “hel”. If the check passes, TechHub gathers extensive information from the infected host. This data is then encrypted and sent to the repository. After transmitting the device information, the process concludes by updating the body of the previously created issue from “hel” to “hey” using PATCH /issues/[issue number] . The malware is now fully prepared to receive commands from the repository. TechHub supports four commands. The commands employ various techniques, such as DLL injection, reflective loading, and section‑mapping injection. ClientHub We also identified a new piece of malware stored in TechHub’s private repository, which we named ClientHub. It supports various commands formed using a bitmask. There are at least two versions of ClientHub: one that communicates with websites via HTTP(S) and one that interacts with the Dropbox API using credentials. The configuration comprises keys and IVs for the SNOW 1.0 algorithm, scheduled execution times, and C2 server addresses encrypted with the SNOW stream cipher. The SNOW cipher is a family of high‑speed stream ciphers used for secure data encryption in telecommunications and wireless networks. This is the first time it has been observed in the malware of the Lazarus Group. To establish C2 communication, the malware initially generates a 32‑byte random array. It subsequently overwrites portions of this array with data collected from the compromised device. The resulting 32‑byte array comprises a blend of random bytes and relevant information. This array is later used as the key for the SNOW algorithm to decrypt data received from the C2 server. Finally, the key array is encrypted with a hard‑coded RSA public key and encoded in Base64. LPEClient LPEClient is the only malware that was also observed in Operation SyncHole, indicating that the actor relies heavily on it for sophisticated victim profiling and payload delivery across multiple operations. LPEClient first appeared in 2019, and was discovered in 2020 . Since then, the tool has been widely observed in the Dream Job and Cascade Hole campaigns that targeted South Korea. Recent research conducted by Check Point revealed that LPEClient was used to deploy the FudModule malware using a zero-day. LPEClient has evolved continuously over time, but we discovered that it recently underwent a major operational revamp. It no longer contains the C2 server address itself; instead, it interacts with ClientHub via a shared buffer. We believe this change is intended to enhance concealment. Timeline of LPEClient The previous version collected the computer name, memory status, CPU specifications, operating system details, version of the ntoskrnl.exe file, firmware table, antivirus name, domain name, user name, the integrity level of the current process, and a random byte sequence of 1,568 bytes. The newly updated LPEClient variant mostly collects the same information; however, it also introduces several changes. It does not collect the version of the ntoskrnl.exe file by querying the FileVersion value. Instead, depending on the specific build, it reads either the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\UBR registry key or the SYSTEM_BUILD_VERSION_INFORMATION structure to retrieve the revision portion of the Windows build number. These values can be used to infer the system’s cumulative update or patch level. To collect information about installed antivirus products, it switched from querying a WQL command to reading the WMI repository file directly. It now reads C:\Windows\System32\wbem\Repository\OBJECTS.DATA and searches for keywords such as AntiVirusProduct, companyName, and displayName to identify the installed products. It also collects low‑level Windows security mitigation states. To achieve this, it queries the SYSTEM_KERNEL_VA_SHADOW_INFORMATION structure for the Kernel VA Shadow mitigation status and the SYSTEM_SHADOW_STACK_INFORMATION structure for the Shadow Stack (CET) protection status. Additionally, it generates a 32‑byte random unique identifier by using the HighwayHash algorithm and an XOR operation with the current system time. The collected information, including the generated identifier, is compressed with the XPRESS Huffman algorithm using the maximum compression setting. The compressed data is then concatenated with the message ID 0xF07D6B34 and encrypted using GOST (also known as Magma), Russia’s national cryptographic standard that employs a DES‑like structure, before being sent to the ClientHub via a shared buffer. Initially, KrCERT described the algorithm as a custom DES‑like scheme. However, further analysis by us and Check Point confirmed that it is actually the GOST algorithm. The key is randomly generated by a proprietary key‑generation algorithm and prepended to the encrypted message. The next request handles the key exchange by delivering the message ID 0xA39CF278 together with the generated unique identifier. The response is decrypted using the AES‑CBC‑256 algorithm. The SHA‑256 hash of the previously generated 1,568‑byte random value, which was originally sent to the C2 server during the collection phase, serves as the key for this decryption. Through this process, LPEClient obtains a byte array comprising four 1,568‑byte blocks from the C2 response. Each block contains an ML‑KEM‑1024 public key, where ML‑KEM is a NIST‑standardized post‑quantum key encapsulation mechanism derived from CRYSTALS‑Kyber. LPEClient then generates four distinct pairs of shared keys and ciphertexts from these blocks, encrypts the ciphertexts with the GOST algorithm, and transmits them to the C2 server via ClientHub together with the message identifier 0xEF8C0D51 and the associated identifier. Now that the preparation phase for receiving payloads is complete, the malware is ready to receive payloads forwarded by ClientHub from the C2 server, along with the necessary parameters. The use of post-quantum cryptography shows that the group intends to hide subsequent payloads. The response to the 0xEF8C0D51 message is decrypted with the Threefish algorithm using a 256-byte key, composed of the four distinct shared keys. Threefish is a tweakable block cipher that accepts a ‘tweak’ value alongside the key and the message. The concept of a tweak is similar to that of a nonce or initialization vector, which are used in different types of ciphers. In LPEClient communication, the tweak for the decryption is derived by XORing the unique identifier with 165 (0xA5) . The first four bytes of the decrypted message must specify the parameter’s length, followed by the parameter itself and then the payload. The payload must be larger than 4 KB and start with the characters 'MZ' , which indicates that the decrypted payload is an executable file. The payload is then reflectively loaded into memory. After successful loading, LPEClient sends the message ID 0xCB790A25 to the C2 server. Before loading the acquired payload, LPEClient takes measures to bypass security products. Instead of invoking VirtualProtect directly, the malware uses the identified HeapPageAllocator::ProtectPages in jscript9.dll to modify the memory page protection of the MD4Update function. The beginning of the function is then overwritten with a hard‑coded opcode sequence that serves as a syscall stub with the required arguments. LPEClient then uses the syscall stub to disable a user‑mode syscall instrumentation hook. We identified the final payload that was ultimately loaded as Cubridge. Interestingly, the start times of these activities align with the earliest evidence we have identified for Operation FlashHole. Although the backdoor was part of the second phase of Operation SyncHole, it has been operating independently with its custom loader since then. These incidents featured malware chains and tools that were distinct from those used in Operation SyncHole and FlashHole. As AhnLab noted in their report , the same backdoor was likely observed in atypical activity, specifically the Gunra ransomware infection. Our investigation further revealed that one instance of a backdoor infection ultimately resulted in the exfiltration of data to a dark web leak site, which clearly differed from Gunra’s. The site appears to have been crafted exclusively for this activity. In summary, unlike other attacks, the backdoor was used in conjunction with both ransomware and data exfiltration. Data leakage site linked to the COPPERHEDGE backdoor on the dark web Another noteworthy point is that the recent Dream Job campaign employs an updated malware chain that, since around 2024, has primarily involved MISTPEN and ForestTiger rather than the earlier arsenal that included tools such as TechHub and Cubridge. However, the updated versions of this older malware have now re-emerged as part of Operation FlashHole. Considering these changes and all aspects of each attack’s TTPs, we have organized a classification for each attack. Overlaps between the recent attacks by Lazarus Group Conclusion Our analysis shows that the Lazarus Group begins preparing for its next operation shortly after completing the previous one, ultimately deploying an enhanced malware chain by refining existing tools. The group continues to use the advanced version of LPEClient for profiling and payload delivery, indicating that the tool is meticulously managed and well maintained. Ironically, the group seems to have adopted more secure post-quantum cryptography faster than many legitimate security products. These observations suggest the involvement of a dedicated developer, with others orchestrating comprehensive attack scenarios against newly targeted software. We anticipated that specialized attacks targeting South Korea would persist. However, we did not foresee multiple attack campaigns being executed simultaneously, each leveraging different types of software and tools. Notably, the COPPERHEDGE cluster appears to be involved in monetizing the attacks, while Operation FlashHole is focused on espionage. We are closely monitoring these changes to understand their motivations and ultimate goals. In October 2025, the South Korean government unveiled a comprehensive cybersecurity plan that will phase out the mandatory installation of security software for users beginning in 2026. We estimate that operations exploiting this software will remain highly active for some time, maximizing efficiency, before the software is fully eliminated or mitigated.
